body:
Why artificial intelligence raises new IP questions

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems can generate text, images, computer code and technical suggestions. This creates questions about whether the output is protected by intellectual property law and, if so, who can claim the relevant rights.

The first distinction is between copyright authorship and patent inventorship. They concern different kinds of intellectual activity and are governed by different legal requirements.

Copyright protects expression

Copyright generally protects qualifying original expressions, such as literary and artistic works, rather than the underlying facts, ideas or general methods. A person may write an original explanation of a scientific fact, but copyright in that explanation does not grant ownership of the scientific fact itself.

India's Copyright Act, 1957, in section 2(d)(vi), addresses authorship of a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work by identifying the author as the person who causes the work to be created.

This statutory wording must be understood carefully in the context of modern generative AI. It does not expressly declare that every unmodified AI output automatically receives copyright protection, nor does it resolve every dispute about identifying the relevant person or the originality of the output.

Where a human makes creative choices, writes substantial original material or makes meaningful expressive changes, those contributions may be relevant to authorship and protection. Whether a particular AI-assisted work qualifies depends on its facts and the applicable law.

Patent law requires a qualifying inventor and invention

A patent protects a qualifying invention rather than merely a creative expression. Under the Patents Act, 1970, patent applications are linked to the true and first inventor or other persons entitled to apply under section 6: an assignee of the right to apply or the legal representative of a deceased person entitled to apply.

India's 2025 Guidelines for Examination of Computer Related Inventions distinguish AI-generated inventions from AI-assisted inventions.

  • AI-generated invention: An invention produced autonomously by AI, or with very limited human intervention. The guidelines state that AI cannot itself be treated as a person who is the true and first inventor under section 6.
  • AI-assisted invention: An invention developed with AI used as a tool. Such an invention is not automatically excluded merely because AI was used. The human inventor's contribution, statutory patentability requirements and the claimed technical application remain relevant.

The 2025 guidelines are examination guidance. They help explain how the patent office approaches applications, but they do not replace the Patents Act.

Why the distinction matters

QuestionCopyrightPatent
What is considered?Qualifying original expressionA qualifying technical invention
Relevant human roleAuthorship and expressive contributionInventorship and inventive contribution
Does AI use automatically defeat protection?No blanket conclusion follows merely from AI assistanceNo blanket exclusion applies merely because AI assisted
Does AI automatically become the rights-holder?NoNo

Simple applications

If a student writes an original educational article and uses AI to improve grammar, the use of AI does not erase the student's original writing. The relevant copyright question concerns the protected expression and human authorship.

If an engineer uses an AI tool to evaluate several technical alternatives and then develops a qualifying new technical solution through inventive human contribution, AI assistance does not by itself make that solution unpatentable. The application must still satisfy the ordinary patent requirements and applicable exclusions.

If an AI system independently produces a technical proposal without an identifiable human inventor, the issue is different. Naming the AI system as the inventor is not supported by the stated Indian patent-examination guidance.

Other questions may arise when AI systems are trained using existing books, images, software or databases. The legal treatment depends on the rights in the material, the nature of its use, applicable exceptions and licensing arrangements. A general statement that all training uses are automatically permitted or prohibited would be inaccurate.

Prelims focus

  • Copyright Act, 1957, section 2(d)(vi): Defines the author of specified computer-generated works as the person who causes the work to be created.
  • Patents Act, 1970, section 6: Addresses persons entitled to apply for patents, including the true and first inventor.
  • 2025 CRI Guidelines: Distinguish AI-generated and AI-assisted inventions.
  • AI assistance does not automatically exclude a qualifying human invention from patent protection.
  • Trap: The author of a copyrighted work and the inventor of a patented invention are not necessarily the same person or legal category.

[Government of India, Copyright Act, 1957, section 2(d)(vi); Government of India, Patents Act, 1970, sections 2 and 6; Intellectual Property India, Guidelines for Examination of Computer Related Inventions, 2025, sections 1.4 and 5.2.1, particularly the discussion of AI inventorship on printed p. 46, consulted 14 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, 'Basics of Copyright', consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Copyright assesses original expression and authorship; patents assess technical inventions and human inventorship, with distinct rules for AI involvement.
pictures.caption: Copyright authorship and patent inventorship assess different kinds of human contribution.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property: Authorship and Inventorship

body:
How software can be protected

Computer software combines instructions, algorithms, code and sometimes valuable technical methods. The legal protection of these elements is not identical.

Copyright can protect qualifying original software code as a literary work. Section 2(o) of India's Copyright Act, 1957, includes computer programmes within the definition of literary works. Copyright protects the relevant expression of the program, not every underlying idea or mathematical method used by it.

For example, 2 programmers may independently write different code to perform the same general calculation. Copyright protection for one programmer's original code does not automatically prevent the other programmer from implementing the same underlying idea independently.

Can software be patented in India?

Section 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970, excludes mathematical methods, business methods, computer programmes per se and algorithms from patentability.

The expression per se is important. Indian patent examination does not treat every invention involving a computer as automatically excluded. A claim must be examined in substance, including whether it concerns a qualifying technical invention rather than merely an excluded computer program or algorithm.

Under the 2025 Guidelines for Examination of Computer Related Inventions, the claimed technical contribution or technical effect is relevant to examining computer-related inventions. Simply describing an ordinary program as an invention, or implementing an abstract method on a generic computer, is not enough by itself.

Software distinction: Original code may receive copyright protection. A patent claim involving software must independently satisfy patentability requirements and overcome the section 3(k) exclusion.

Data, databases and intellectual property

Data refers to recorded facts, measurements or other information. A database is an organized collection of such material.

A raw fact does not automatically become someone's copyright property merely because it has been collected. However, an original database or compilation may qualify for copyright protection where the applicable originality requirements are met. India's Copyright Act expressly recognizes tables and compilations, including computer databases, within literary works.

The distinction can be illustrated through rainfall observations. The fact that a particular location received a certain amount of rainfall is not itself a copyrightable literary expression. An original database structure, explanatory text or other qualifying creative arrangement may involve separate rights.

Control over data may also depend on contracts, confidentiality obligations and personal-data protection law. These are not identical to copyright. A dataset may be accessible but subject to conditions on copying, redistribution or use.

When data is used to train AI systems, separate questions arise about permission to access material, copyright in protected content, licence terms and the treatment of personal information. The legal answer depends on the facts and applicable rules.

What does open source mean?

Open-source software is distributed under a licence allowing users to access its source code and exercise specified rights to use, modify and redistribute the software.

The presence of source code on a website does not automatically make the software open source. The licence must grant the relevant permissions. Likewise, open-source software is not necessarily in the public domain: copyright commonly remains in place and the licence defines permitted uses.

TypeGeneral approachImportant condition
Permissive open-source licenceAllows broad reuse, modification and redistributionTypically requires preservation of specified copyright notices or licence conditions
Copyleft open-source licenceAllows reuse and modification while preserving specified freedoms for recipientsDistribution of covered modified software may trigger source-code and same-licence obligations
Public-domain softwareNot subject to the relevant exclusive copyright restrictionsNot the same legal category as copyrighted open-source software

Common examples of permissive licences include MIT and BSD licences. The GNU General Public License (GPL) is an important copyleft licence.

Under ordinary GPL conditions, a person may generally modify covered software privately without being required to publish those changes to everyone. Distribution to recipients is the important event that can trigger corresponding source-code and licensing obligations. Exact obligations depend on the licence and how the software is used.

Open source and innovation

Open-source development can support technology transfer by allowing researchers, students and businesses to study and improve existing software. It may reduce the need to recreate programs independently and enable collaboration.

Nevertheless, open-source licensing does not automatically remove all patent, privacy, trademark or confidentiality questions. A company must consider the rights and obligations relevant to its particular product.

Prelims focus

  • Copyright Act, 1957, section 2(o): Computer programmes are included within literary works.
  • Patents Act, 1970, section 3(k): Excludes computer programmes per se and algorithms, among other categories.
  • Individual facts and a qualifying original database are not the same subject of protection.
  • MIT and BSD: Common permissive open-source licence families.
  • GPL: A commonly used copyleft licence.
  • Trap: Open-source software is not automatically public-domain software or software without licence conditions.

[Government of India, Copyright Act, 1957, section 2(o); Government of India, Patents Act, 1970, section 3(k); Intellectual Property India, Guidelines for Examination of Computer Related Inventions, 2025, sections addressing patentable subject matter and technical effect, consulted 14 November 2026; Open Source Initiative, 'The Open Source Definition', consulted 14 November 2026; GNU Project, GNU GPL Frequently Asked Questions, sections on private modifications and distribution, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A digital product connects to copyright, patent law, licence conditions and privacy obligations, with different rules for code, data and reuse.
pictures.caption: Software code, data and licensing arrangements can involve different legal rights.

title: Software, Data and Open Source: Different Forms of Intellectual Property Protection

body:
Biotechnology and the boundary of patent protection

Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or biological components to develop products and processes. Its applications include agriculture, medicine and industrial production. Intellectual property issues arise when research uses natural biological material, existing traditional knowledge or newly developed technical methods.

The key legal distinction is between discovering something that already exists in nature and developing a qualifying invention.

For example, identifying a naturally occurring plant with a known traditional use does not make that plant or use a new invention. A researcher may nevertheless develop a genuinely new technical process involving biological material. Whether that process can be patented depends on novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability and the relevant statutory exclusions.

India's Patents Act is particularly important here:

  • Section 3(c): Excludes the mere discovery of something occurring in nature.
  • Section 3(j): Excludes plants and animals in whole or in part, other than microorganisms, including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animals.
  • Section 3(p): Excludes traditional knowledge and mere duplication or aggregation of known traditional properties.

Even where a qualifying biotechnology invention is possible, the researcher may still need to comply with biodiversity access, disclosure and benefit-sharing requirements. A patent and lawful access to a resource are separate matters.

What is a patent thicket?

A patent thicket is a situation in which numerous overlapping or closely related patent rights create difficulties for developing or commercializing a technology.

A modern product may use several patented components or methods owned by different parties. An organization wishing to manufacture the product may therefore need to identify relevant patents and obtain more than one licence.

Patent thickets can arise in complex technology sectors, including information technology and some biotechnology fields. They may increase legal costs, delay development or make it difficult for smaller organizations to enter a market.

Ways to address overlapping patent rights

  • Licensing: A patent holder permits another party to use a protected invention under agreed conditions.
  • Cross-licensing: Two or more parties grant each other rights to use specified patents.
  • Patent pools: Multiple patent holders make selected patent rights available through a coordinated licensing arrangement.
  • Alternative development: A developer may seek a lawful technical approach that does not require using a particular protected invention.

Licensing and patent pools can support technology transfer, but their benefits depend on their terms and competition-law considerations. A patent thicket does not mean that all the patents involved are invalid.

Putting the concepts together

Consider a hypothetical research project in which a business learns about a traditionally used medicinal plant from a community in Gujarat and develops a commercial product.

  1. Identify the existing knowledge: Determine what is already known about the plant and its traditional uses. Existing published or otherwise legally relevant knowledge may constitute prior art.
  2. Check lawful access: Determine whether collecting the plant or obtaining associated knowledge requires permission, intimation or approval under biodiversity law.
  3. Consider community interests: Identify applicable benefit-sharing obligations and any relevant agreements with knowledge-holders or benefit claimers.
  4. Examine the invention: A known traditional use cannot be presented as a new patentable invention. A genuinely new technical process must still satisfy the Patents Act and applicable exclusions.
  5. Make required disclosures: The patent application must contain the applicable information about the source and geographical origin of biological material.
  6. Address commercialization: Relevant licences, overlapping patents and any further biodiversity-law requirements must be considered before commercial use.

This example shows why intellectual property protection is not a single question of who first files a patent. The law distinguishes existing knowledge, an applicant's inventive contribution, lawful access, community interests and the rights needed to commercialize a product.

Connections across the whole subtopic

Traditional knowledge, emerging technology and intellectual property can be understood through 4 connected distinctions:

  • Existing knowledge versus a new invention: Prior art, TKDL and section 3(p) help prevent unjustified patents over known practices.
  • Permission versus benefit sharing: Biodiversity law, local institutions, PIC and MAT address lawful access and the conditions of use.
  • Expression versus technical invention: Copyright authorship and patent inventorship are different, including when AI is used.
  • Exclusive rights versus permitted reuse: Software licences, open-source terms and multiple overlapping patents shape technology transfer.

Central distinction: A lawful commercial product may require several independent conditions to be satisfied. Evidence of traditional prior art does not itself settle benefit sharing, and a valid patent does not eliminate access-law or licensing obligations.

Prelims focus

  • Section 3(c): Mere discovery of something occurring in nature is excluded from patentability.
  • Section 3(j): Important exclusions concerning plants, animals and essentially biological processes.
  • Section 3(p): Traditional knowledge exclusion.
  • Patent thicket: Multiple overlapping patent rights affecting a technology.
  • Cross-licensing: Reciprocal permission to use specified patents.
  • Trap: A valid patent does not automatically establish legal access to biological material, freedom from other patents or compliance with benefit-sharing requirements.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapters 11–12, 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes' and 'Biotechnology and Its Applications', especially section 12.4; Government of India, Patents Act, 1970, sections 3 and 10; National Biodiversity Authority, FAQs on access and intellectual property applications under the amended Biological Diversity Act, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, 'Standards and Patents', sections concerning patent pools and licensing, consulted 14 November 2026; WHO, WIPO and WTO, 'Promoting Access to Medical Technologies and Innovation', discussion of patent thickets and licensing, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Several patent rights may affect the commercialization of one complex product.
